claims.text: Body-centered-cubic refractory high-entropy alloys can have a significant energetic driving force for chemical short-range order.
Percolating SRO clusters induce a non-monotonic transition in thermal conductivity in single-phase bcc refractory high-entropy alloys.
At low SRO volume fraction, enhanced phonon scattering reduces thermal conductivity.
Above a critical SRO volume fraction, connected SRO clusters increase thermal conductivity.
Percolating SRO clusters form coherent, low-scattering pathways through the disordered matrix.
Chemical ordering within SRO clusters reduces mass-fluctuation scattering.
The percolating SRO network alters the phonon mean-free-path distribution.
Connectivity of the SRO network, rather than additive scattering by isolated clusters, drives the conductivity transition.
Standard serial, parallel, rule-of-mixtures, or effective-medium models predict a monotonic conductivity decrease with increasing SRO.
Standard interatomic potentials may fail to reproduce SRO evolution accurately in refractory high-entropy alloys.
The potential energy surface used for modeling must accurately represent the energetic driving forces for chemical clustering and SRO evolution.
Controlled thermal aging or rapid quenching can be used to tune SRO and target formation of a percolating cluster network.
The alloy remains single-phase bcc above 1000 K while SRO clustering is favorable and phase separation is suppressed.
Thermal conductivity has a minimum at the SRO percolation threshold and increases after the network becomes connected.
The resulting conductivity differs significantly from serial or parallel mixing-model predictions.
The proposed percolative transition occurs only when SRO clusters can grow without secondary-phase precipitation.
The percolative transition is unlikely in fcc systems or multiphase alloys where phase separation dominates.
The percolation threshold and magnitude of the conductivity increase depend on the interatomic potential used to model SRO.
Diffuse-scattering intensity and correlation length from high-temperature X-ray and neutron scattering can identify atomic-scale SRO percolation.
A monotonic conductivity decrease with increasing SRO would falsify the proposed non-monotonic percolation mechanism.
